title: 2 Samuel 2:24–32
context: Joab and Abishai pursue Abner. The sun goes down when they come to the hill of Ammah, which lies before Giah by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon. The children of Benjamin gather after Abner as one band and stand on the top of a hill. Abner calls to Joab: shall the sword devour forever, and does he not know that it will be bitterness in the latter end, and how long before he asks the people to return from following their brothers? Joab answers that, as God lives, if Abner had not spoken, the people would have gone on until morning, each following his brother. Joab blows the trumpet; the people stand still, pursue Israel no more, and fight no more. Abner and his men go all that night through the Arabah, cross the Jordan, go through all Bithron, and come to Mahanaim. Joab, gathering the people, finds nineteen of David’s men and Asahel missing; David’s servants have struck Benjamin and Abner’s men so that three hundred sixty died. They take up Asahel and bury him in his father’s tomb in Bethlehem; Joab and his men go all night, and the day breaks on them at Hebron. Both traditions read the unit as the halt of a civil pursuit, the return of the dead, and the two companies going back to their seats. The place names are given as the WEB spells them. The scene is narrative, not a type of some later peace or altar.

verses.text: But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. The sun went down when they had come to the hill of Ammah, that lies before Giah by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon.
verses.arminianNotes:
But Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. The sun went down when they had come to the hill of Ammah, that lies before Giah by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon. The two remaining brothers take up the chase as far as a named hill at sundown.

Arminian readers hear the pursuit continuing after Asahel’s death, now by Joab and Abishai, to a place the narrator locates with care: the hill of Ammah, before Giah, by the way of the wilderness of Gibeon. The sites are not further identified here, and they should not be fixed as if a consensus had settled them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the sunset and the named hill as the end of that day’s running. Joab and Abishai are still after Abner; the geography is given as the WEB gives it, without a typological reading of the wilderness or the hill.

Both traditions read the verse as the setting of the halt that is about to be called, shared narrative ground.

verses.text: The children of Benjamin gathered themselves together after Abner and became one band, and stood on the top of a hill.
verses.arminianNotes:
The children of Benjamin gathered themselves together after Abner and became one band, and stood on the top of a hill. Abner is no longer a lone fugitive; Benjamin forms a band and holds a height.

Arminian readers hear a rally. The tribe that stands with Ishbosheth gathers after its captain, becomes one band, and takes the top of a hill, a position from which Abner can now speak.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same gathering and the same stand on the height. Benjamin’s unity in this moment gives Abner a body of men behind him when he calls to Joab.

Both traditions take the verse as the northern rally, descriptive, not a symbol of some later remnant or hill.

verses.text: Then Abner called to Joab, and said, “Shall the sword devour forever? Don’t you know that it will be bitterness in the latter end? How long will it be then, before you ask the people to return from following their brothers?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Then Abner called to Joab, and said, “Shall the sword devour forever? Don’t you know that it will be bitterness in the latter end? How long will it be then, before you ask the people to return from following their brothers?”

Arminian readers hear a plea to stop a brother-war. The sword, the bitterness in the end, and the “brothers” are Abner’s own words. He asks Joab to call the people back; the next verse will show that the asking itself is what Joab was waiting for.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the three questions as a real appeal to end the pursuit. “Shall the sword devour forever?” names the cost of going on; “their brothers” names the civil character of the fight.

Both traditions read the verse as the call that stops the day, shared ground, without treating Abner’s speech as either pure cunning or pure repentance as if the text had decided that.

verses.text: Joab said, “As God lives, if you had not spoken, surely then in the morning the people would have gone away, and not each followed his brother.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab said, “As God lives, if you had not spoken, surely then in the morning the people would have gone away, and not each followed his brother.” Joab answers with an oath and a claim about what would have happened.

Arminian readers hear Joab putting the halt on Abner’s word. If Abner had not spoken, the pursuit, Joab says, would have gone until morning. He does not deny the bitterness Abner named; he says the speech is what stopped him from letting it run on.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the oath “As God lives” and the same counterfactual: without Abner’s speaking, the people would have followed each brother until morning. Joab presents himself as ready to stop once that word is said, and the next verse will show him stopping the army.

Both traditions take the verse as Joab’s reply, descriptive of how the cease-fire is framed, not as a fork over the oath itself.

verses.text: So Joab blew the trumpet; and all the people stood still and pursued Israel no more, and they fought no more.
verses.arminianNotes:
So Joab blew the trumpet; and all the people stood still and pursued Israel no more, and they fought no more. The signal is given, and the fighting of that day ends.

Arminian readers hear a real stop. The trumpet is enough; the people stand still, the pursuit of Israel ceases, and they fight no more. The civil battle is suspended by a commander’s horn.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the blowing of the trumpet as the act that fulfills the exchange of verses 26–27. Pursuit and fighting both cease; the two companies will now go their ways.

Both traditions read the verse as the end of the engagement, shared narrative ground.

verses.text: Abner and his men went all that night through the Arabah; and they passed over the Jordan, and went through all Bithron, and came to Mahanaim.
verses.arminianNotes:
Abner and his men went all that night through the Arabah; and they passed over the Jordan, and went through all Bithron, and came to Mahanaim. The northern force retreats by night to the city from which it had come.

Arminian readers hear a long, night march: the Arabah, the Jordan, all Bithron, and at last Mahanaim, Ishbosheth’s seat. Bithron is a name the text does not explain; it should not be located more firmly than the verse allows.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same night withdrawal, back across the Jordan to Mahanaim. Abner’s band is not destroyed; it returns to its base after the beating and the halt.

Both traditions take the verse as the northern return, with the place names as the WEB spells them, and without typological pressure on the crossing.

verses.text: Joab returned from following Abner; and when he had gathered all the people together, nineteen men of David’s and Asahel were missing.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joab returned from following Abner; and when he had gathered all the people together, nineteen men of David’s and Asahel were missing. The southern loss is counted: nineteen, and Asahel besides.

Arminian readers hear a careful tally after the trumpet. Joab gathers the people and finds those nineteen missing, and Asahel, whose death has already been told. The cost on David’s side is small beside the next verse, and it is not zero.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the gathering and the count as the narrator’s way of closing the day for David’s servants. Asahel is named apart from the nineteen; the beloved brother’s body is still to be carried home.

Both traditions read the verse as a casualty notice, shared ground, not a riddle about the arithmetic.

verses.text: But David’s servants had struck Benjamin and Abner’s men so that three hundred sixty men died.
verses.arminianNotes:
But David’s servants had struck Benjamin and Abner’s men so that three hundred sixty men died. The northern dead are many more than the missing of verse 30.

Arminian readers hear the severity of the battle already called “very severe” in verse 17. Three hundred sixty of Benjamin and Abner’s men die; the beaten side pays the heavier price that day.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same contrast, the “But”: David’s servants have struck, and the dead on Abner’s side are three hundred sixty. The figures stand as given, without being turned into a moral of easy triumph; Asahel is still among the southern dead.

Both traditions take the verse as the count of the northern fallen, descriptive and shared.

verses.text: They took up Asahel and buried him in the tomb of his father, which was in Bethlehem. Joab and his men went all night, and the day broke on them at Hebron.
verses.arminianNotes:
They took up Asahel and buried him in the tomb of his father, which was in Bethlehem. Joab and his men went all night, and the day broke on them at Hebron. The dead brother is laid in the family tomb, and the living return to the city of David’s anointing.

Arminian readers hear a burial at Bethlehem, Asahel’s father’s tomb, and then a night march that ends at Hebron at daybreak. The chapter closes where David’s Judahite reign is seated, with a brother’s grave behind them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the burial in Bethlehem and the dawn at Hebron as the last movements of the day. Joab brings the men home to the city the LORD had named; Asahel rests in his father’s tomb.

Both traditions read the verse as the close of the unit, shared narrative ground, without forcing a typological meaning onto Bethlehem or the breaking day.
